extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy / classical economics
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition of the economic principles determining differences in wages and profits across occupations and countries, including the mechanisms that equalize returns and the five main circumstances that cause wage variation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proportion of interest to ordinary rate of clear profit
rubrics_metrics.description: The usual market rate of interest ought to bear a variable proportion to the ordinary rate of clear profit; this proportion changes as profit rises or falls (e.g., 'double interest' in Great Britain is regarded as a good/moderate profit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where ordinary clear profit is 8–10%, it may be reasonable for about one half to go to interest when business is carried on with borrowed money; stock is at the borrower's risk and interest compensates that risk (an example: 4–5% may be sufficient recompense). The proportion will differ in countries with much lower or higher ordinary profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: High profits raise commodity prices more than high wages
rubrics_metrics.description: A rise in profits tends to raise the price of commodities more strongly than a rise in wages: wages add arithmetically through stages of production, while profit compounds geometrically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example in linen manufacture: a small per-day wage rise raises price only by the cumulative twopences equal to workers×days (arithmetic), but a percentage rise in profit applies successively at each stage, growing like compound interest. Merchants complain about high wages but are silent about the pernicious effects of high profits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tendency toward equality of advantages across employments
rubrics_metrics.description: In the same neighbourhood, advantages and disadvantages of different employments will tend to equality because people will move into more advantageous occupations and abandon less advantageous ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This equalization presumes perfect liberty and freedom to choose and change occupations; deviations arise partly from circumstances inherent to occupations and partly from policy that restricts perfect liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreeableness or disagreeableness of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages vary with the pleasantness, hardship, cleanliness, or honour of the employment (agreeable jobs pay less; disagreeable or dishonourable ones tend to pay more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: journeyman tailor (easier) earns less than journeyman weaver; collier (dirty/dangerous) earns more than journeyman blacksmith; butcher (odious trade) often more profitable; public executioner is highly paid per unit of work. The same principle affects profits of stock in disagreeable trades (innkeeper example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Easiness and expense of learning the trade (education/apprenticeship costs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages of labour are higher where the trade requires costly, time-consuming education or apprenticeship because the worker must recoup the investment in learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: a skilled worker is like an expensive machine whose extraordinary output must replace the capital laid out on it; therefore skilled mechanics and manufacturers earn somewhat higher wages to compensate education expense. The text notes European apprenticeship systems and contrasts with country labour where learning occurs while working (hence smaller premium). Profits of stock appear little affected by learning costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constancy or inconstancy of employment
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages vary with how steady employment in the trade is; inconstant employment commands higher wages to compensate for idle periods and uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: masons and bricklayers (work interrupted by weather) earn from 1.5× to double common labour wages; journeymen tailors in London face irregular work and higher wages; when inconstancy combines with hardship (e.g., coal-heavers), wages can be many times common labour. Constancy of employment does not similarly affect ordinary profits of stock in a trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of trust required in the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Wages are higher for occupations that require trust because society must place those workers in a social rank commensurate with that trust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: goldsmiths and jewellers, physicians, lawyers receive higher pay due to entrusted valuable materials, health, fortune, or reputation; combined with long and costly education, trust further raises remuneration. When a person employs only their own stock there is no such trust premium for profit rates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability or improbability of success in an occupation
rubrics_metrics.description: Occupations where success is improbable (e.g., liberal professions) reward the few successful practitioners with high retribution to compensate for many failures; those occupations thus have high potential rewards to offset the 'unfair lottery' of success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: many students of law fail to make a living, so the small number who succeed must gain enough to compensate the unsuccessful many; this makes professions appear under-recompensed on average. Non-monetary rewards (reputation, admiration) also attract entrants despite low average pecuniary gains. Performers receive high pay because of rarity and social discredit of commercializing talents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of risk on ordinary profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Ordinary rates of profit rise with the risk or uncertainty of returns in a branch of trade, but not necessarily enough to fully compensate the risk (i.e., not proportional).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Inland trades are generally less risky than foreign trades; among foreign trades some routes (e.g., to Jamaica) are riskier than others (e.g., to North America). Hazardous trades (smuggling) can be most profitable when successful but lead often to bankruptcies; competition and over-entrance into risky trades tend to reduce average profits below what would fully compensate risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apparent profit may be disguised wages or necessary compensation
rubrics_metrics.description: Some high observed profit-margins are really remuneration for skill, trust, or the smallness/narrowness of a business and should be considered as wages rather than pure profit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: apothecaries' large markups on drugs often pay for skill and trust (physician of the poor); a small grocer can make 40–50% on a small stock because he must read, write, account, judge many goods, and perform the functions of a great merchant but without capital — the high percentage on small capital does not mean extravagant true profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative rates of profit and wages affect international price competitiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Differences in ordinary rates of profit and wages between countries influence commodity prices and international competitiveness; low profits can compensate for high wages and allow cheaper exports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In countries rapidly advancing to riches, low rates of profit may, in the price of many commodities, offset high wages and enable them to sell as cheap as less thriving neighbours where wages are lower. The prior point that profits compound (raising prices) informs this effect.
